// Every subtest here is handed a callback that was bound to a name first. The
// closure is the same object graph as the inline spelling and fails the same
// way -- the diagnostic is filed against the parent and the subtest reports
// "subtest may have called FailNow on a parent test" -- and a rule that requires
// the argument to be an inline function literal reports none of them.
package fixture

import (
	"testing"

	qt "github.com/frankban/quicktest"
)

func TestNamedSubtestCallback(t *testing.T) {
	c := qt.New(t)

	borrowsChecker := func(t *testing.T) {
		c.Assert(1, qt.Equals, 1)
	}
	t.Run("named callback borrowing the parent checker", borrowsChecker)

	borrowsTB := func(subT *testing.T) {
		subT.Log("the parameter is not the TB this checker is built from")
		inner := qt.New(t)
		inner.Assert(2, qt.Equals, 2)
	}
	t.Run("named callback building a checker from the parent TB", borrowsTB)

	// The target shape, written with a named callback. Nothing crosses the
	// boundary, so nothing is reported.
	ownsChecker := func(t *testing.T) {
		own := qt.New(t)
		own.Assert(3, qt.Equals, 3)
	}
	t.Run("named callback that owns its checker", ownsChecker)
}

// c is a package-level counter, and it is spelled c on purpose: the callback
// below reads it, and a rule that read a file-scope callback's body against the
// scope of whichever test called it would report it as the caller's checker.
var c = 0

var packaged = func(t *testing.T) {
	own := qt.New(t)
	own.Assert(c, qt.Equals, 0)
}

// A callback named at file scope cannot see any test function's locals, so
// nothing here crosses a boundary even though the caller has its own c.
func TestFileScopeCallback(t *testing.T) {
	c := qt.New(t)
	c.Check(5, qt.Equals, 5)

	t.Run("callback named at file scope", packaged)
}

func BenchmarkNamedSubtestCallback(b *testing.B) {
	c := qt.New(b)

	borrows := func(b *testing.B) {
		c.Assert(4, qt.Equals, 4)
	}
	b.Run("named subbenchmark callback", borrows)
}

func FuzzNamedTarget(f *testing.F) {
	c := qt.New(f)

	borrows := func(t *testing.T, input string) {
		c.Assert(input, qt.Not(qt.Equals), "")
	}
	f.Fuzz(borrows)
}

// A callback copied into a second name is the same literal. Stopping at the
// declaration that has no literal of its own made `alias := callback` a
// one-line rename out of the rule, on the same shape the file above catches.
func TestAliasedNamedCallback(t *testing.T) {
	c := qt.New(t)

	borrows := func(t *testing.T) {
		c.Assert(6, qt.Equals, 6)
	}
	alias := borrows
	t.Run("the alias is the same callback", alias)
}

// And the negative: an alias of a callback that borrows nothing stays silent,
// so following the chain cannot become a source of findings of its own.
func TestAliasedConformingCallback(t *testing.T) {
	owns := func(t *testing.T) {
		c := qt.New(t)
		c.Assert(7, qt.Equals, 7)
	}
	alias := owns
	t.Run("the alias of a conforming callback is conforming", alias)
}

// A callback rebound before the call has no single known value, so the literal
// its declaration was given is not what the call receives. Following the
// initializer anyway reports a subtest that is conforming at the only place it
// is used, which is the direction a gate with no baseline may not fail in.
func TestReassignedCallbackIsNotItsFirstLiteral(t *testing.T) {
	c := qt.New(t)

	cb := func(t *testing.T) {
		c.Assert(8, qt.Equals, 8)
	}
	cb = func(t *testing.T) {
		inner := qt.New(t)
		inner.Assert(9, qt.Equals, 9)
	}
	t.Run("the callback the call receives is conforming", cb)
}

// And the same thing one alias further out, where the name the call names was
// rebound and the name it was copied from was not.
func TestReassignedAliasIsNotItsFirstLiteral(t *testing.T) {
	c := qt.New(t)

	borrows := func(t *testing.T) {
		c.Assert(10, qt.Equals, 10)
	}
	alias := borrows
	alias = func(t *testing.T) {
		inner := qt.New(t)
		inner.Assert(11, qt.Equals, 11)
	}
	t.Run("the alias the call receives is conforming", alias)
}
